copy.title: From silicon to software
copy.lede: A path from a flashlight signal to the phones, machines, networks, money and AI systems of today, covering every layer in between. Each square below is one step. Light them all and there’s very little in modern technology you won’t be able to explain.
copy.legend: Numbers are phases. Gold squares are finished, half-gold are started, the ringed one is next, and dashed ones are advanced steps.

intros.path: Every step works the same way. Watch or read the resources, build the small thing if there is one, then answer the checkpoint out loud as if teaching a friend. If you can’t, go back before moving on: ticks mean you finished something, checkpoints mean you understood it. Big topics are split into Basics and Advanced steps. Turn on “Basics first” to take a lighter pass through everything, then come back for depth. The full path is several years of part-time study, and that’s normal. If you prefer hands-on work, Part 7, on devices, vehicles and medical systems, can start once you’ve finished Part 4.
intros.patterns: LeetCode’s thousands of problems are built on a couple of dozen patterns. Each one below explains the idea, why it’s worth knowing, where it runs in real software, and how to recognize it in a problem statement. You don’t need to solve a problem to understand what it’s asking and why it matters. Practice links open on LeetCode.
intros.concepts: Heard a term in the news, at work or in a video, or wondering how some device works? Search here to see what it means and which steps teach it.

copy.linksNote: Video links open a YouTube search, because exact titles change and channels reorganize. Books open a library search so you can find a copy. Courses and articles link to their home pages.

ATLAS.line: Remember what you’ve seen so you never search twice.
ATLAS.idea: A hash function turns a key, like a word or an ID, into an array position. Storing items there makes “have I seen this?” and “what goes with this key?” nearly instant.
ATLAS.why: It turns many “check every pair” solutions from O(n²) into a single O(n) pass, by trading memory for speed.
where: Python dictionaries, JavaScript objects and sets
Caches like Redis and Memcached, which are huge hash tables over a network
Database hash indexes and hash joins
Compilers’ symbol tables, which map variable names to their details
Deduplicating files and detecting repeated data
ATLAS.spot: “Find a pair that…”, “has this appeared before”, “count how often”, “group things that share a property”.

ATLAS.line: Walk two positions through the data so each element is visited once.
ATLAS.idea: Keep two indexes, often one at each end or one moving faster than the other, and move them based on what you see. In sorted data, each step rules out many possibilities at once.
ATLAS.why: It replaces nested loops with one pass, and usually needs no extra memory.
where: The merge step of merge sort
Merge joins in databases, which walk two sorted tables side by side
Removing duplicates or filtering data in place
Comparing two sorted lists, like finding common contacts
ATLAS.spot: Sorted input, “find a pair or triple adding up to”, “rearrange in place”, palindromes.

ATLAS.line: Keep a running summary of a range as it slides along.
ATLAS.idea: Maintain a contiguous range with a left and right edge. Grow it on one side and shrink it on the other, updating a running total or count, instead of recomputing every range from scratch.
ATLAS.why: Questions about the best substring or subarray drop from O(n²) or worse to O(n).
where: Rate limiters that cap requests per minute
TCP’s sliding window, which controls how much data is in flight on a connection
Moving averages on stock charts and monitoring dashboards
Compression like gzip, which looks back over a sliding window for repeated text
ATLAS.spot: “Contiguous”, “longest or shortest substring”, “subarray with at most k…”, “in the last n items”.
pr: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

ATLAS.line: Last in, first out: the shape of anything nested.
ATLAS.idea: Push items on and pop them off the top. Anything that opens must close in reverse order, which is exactly what a stack tracks. A monotonic stack keeps items in sorted order to answer “what’s the next bigger thing?” in one pass.
ATLAS.why: It matches nesting and “come back to this later” structure naturally.
where: The call stack that runs every function call in every program
Undo in editors, and the back button in browsers
Parsing brackets, HTML, JSON and code
Calculators and compilers evaluating expressions
ATLAS.spot: Matching brackets, “next greater or smaller element”, evaluating expressions, undoing the most recent thing.

ATLAS.line: First in, first out, in a fixed loop of memory.
ATLAS.idea: A queue hands items out in the order they arrived. A ring buffer stores a queue in a fixed-size array whose ends wrap around, so it never allocates memory or shifts items.
ATLAS.why: It lets a fast producer and a slower consumer work at their own pace, with fixed memory and predictable timing, which matters a lot in hardware.
where: Serial drivers buffering bytes between an interrupt and the main program
Audio and video playback buffers
Network cards handing packets to the operating system
Keyboard buffers, and logs that keep only the latest entries
Message queues between services
ATLAS.spot: “Design a circular queue”, “first come, first served”, “keep the last k items”, processing in arrival order.

ATLAS.line: Precompute running totals so any range sum is one subtraction.
ATLAS.idea: Store the total of everything up to each position. The sum of any range is then the total at its end minus the total just before its start.
ATLAS.why: Repeated range questions become O(1) each after one O(n) pass.
where: Summed-area tables in image processing, used in classic face detection
Cumulative totals in analytics and finance dashboards
Fast blurring and box filters in graphics
ATLAS.spot: “Sum of a subarray”, many range queries on data that doesn’t change, “subarray summing to k”.

ATLAS.line: Items joined by pointers instead of sitting side by side.
ATLAS.idea: Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next. Inserting or removing at a known spot is cheap; jumping to the 500th item is slow. A fast and a slow pointer moving at different speeds detect loops and find midpoints.
ATLAS.why: These problems teach you to reason about pointers, which is how memory really links things together.
where: LRU caches, which pair a hash map with a doubly linked list
Lists of tasks and memory blocks inside operating system kernels
Blockchains, where each block points to the one before it
Cycle detection in algorithms that factor large numbers
ATLAS.spot: “Reverse”, “merge”, “detect a cycle”, “find the middle”, or any problem handed a ListNode.

ATLAS.line: Halve the possibilities with every question.
ATLAS.idea: In sorted data, or any yes/no condition that flips once, check the middle and throw away the half that can’t contain the answer. A billion items take about 30 steps.
ATLAS.why: It turns O(n) searches into O(log n), and “binary search on the answer” cracks many optimization problems.
where: git bisect, which finds the commit that introduced a bug
Searching inside database index pages
Looking up words in a sorted dictionary or file
Finding the largest setting that still fits a limit, like batch size in memory
ATLAS.spot: Sorted input, “minimum value such that…”, “maximum that still works”, a required O(log n) time.
pr: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

ATLAS.line: Put things in order, and many hard problems become easy.
ATLAS.idea: Sorting groups equal items, puts neighbors next to each other and makes binary search possible. Most practical sorts take O(n log n).
ATLAS.why: Sorting first is often the trick that turns an O(n²) problem into an O(n log n) one.
where: ORDER BY in every database, including external sorts for data bigger than memory
Python’s and Java’s built-in sorts, based on Timsort, a merge sort and insertion sort hybrid
Ranking search results and feeds
Drawing 3D scenes back to front
ATLAS.spot: “Kth largest”, “arrange so that…”, “group together”, or a problem that gets easy once things are in order.
pr: Kth Largest Element in an Array

ATLAS.line: Sort ranges by start, then sweep through them.
ATLAS.idea: Represent things as start and end points. After sorting by start, overlaps only happen between neighbors, so one pass can merge, count or compare them.
ATLAS.why: Scheduling and overlap questions turn into a sort plus a single sweep.
where: Calendar apps finding free time and conflicts
Meeting room and resource booking systems
Memory allocators merging adjacent free blocks
Genome analysis and video editing timelines
ATLAS.spot: Pairs of [start, end], “overlapping”, “merge”, “minimum rooms or resources needed”.
pr: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons

ATLAS.line: Treat a number as a row of switches.
ATLAS.idea: Use AND, OR, XOR and shifts to test, set and flip individual bits. XOR has a neat property: anything XORed with itself cancels to zero.
ATLAS.why: It packs data tightly and does work in a single CPU instruction, and it shows you how numbers really sit in hardware.
where: Setting and clearing bits in hardware registers to control microcontroller pins
Unix file permissions, stored as read, write and execute bits
Network subnet masks that pick out part of an IP address
Feature flags and settings packed into one integer
Chess engines representing the board as 64-bit numbers
RAID storage rebuilding a lost disk using XOR parity
ATLAS.spot: “Without extra space”, “appears once while others appear twice”, counting 1 bits, powers of two.

ATLAS.line: Solve a node by first solving its children.
ATLAS.idea: A tree is a hierarchy where each node has children. Most tree problems are recursion: answer the question for the left and right subtrees, then combine. Traversals visit nodes depth-first or level by level.
ATLAS.why: Hierarchies are everywhere, and these problems build your recursion skills.
where: Folders in every file system
The DOM, the tree a browser builds from HTML
Abstract syntax trees inside compilers and interpreters
JSON documents, and decision trees in machine learning
ATLAS.spot: A TreeNode input, “depth”, “path”, “level by level”, “ancestor”.

ATLAS.n: Binary search trees and balanced trees
ATLAS.line: A tree that keeps everything sorted as it changes.
ATLAS.idea: In a binary search tree, everything left of a node is smaller and everything right is larger, so search, insert and delete take O(log n) as long as the tree stays balanced. Real systems use self-balancing versions, and B-trees, a wide and shallow cousin.
ATLAS.why: You get sorted order and fast updates at the same time, which a plain sorted array can’t give you.
where: B-tree and B+tree indexes in almost every database and many file systems
Red-black trees in Linux’s process scheduler

ATLAS.spot: “BST” in the title, “kth smallest”, “validate the ordering”, in-order traversal.

Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST

ATLAS.line: Always get the smallest item fast, without sorting everything.
ATLAS.idea: A heap is a tree packed into an array, where each parent is smaller than its children. You can add an item or take out the minimum in O(log n).
ATLAS.why: “Give me the most urgent item next” is a constant need, and a heap answers it far faster than re-sorting.
where: Job and timer schedulers in operating systems and language runtimes
Dijkstra’s algorithm in map routing
Building Huffman codes for compression
“Top 10” and trending lists over huge data streams
Stock exchange order books, which always match the best buy and sell prices
ATLAS.spot: “Kth largest or smallest”, “top k”, “closest k”, “median of a stream”, “always process the cheapest next”.
pr: Kth Largest Element in a Stream

ATLAS.line: A tree of letters where every path spells a prefix.
ATLAS.idea: Each edge is a character, so all words sharing a prefix share a path from the root. Checking whether any word starts with “inter” takes time proportional to the prefix, not to the size of the dictionary.
ATLAS.why: Prefix questions over large word sets become fast and memory-efficient.
where: Autocomplete in search boxes and phone keyboards
Spell checkers
Internet routers matching IP addresses by longest prefix
ATLAS.spot: “Starts with”, “prefix”, searching many words at once, a dictionary of words.
pr: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure

ATLAS.line: Range questions on data that keeps changing.
ATLAS.idea: Prefix sums break when values change. These trees store partial totals for ranges, so both updates and range queries take O(log n).
ATLAS.why: They handle live data where both reads and writes are frequent. They’re an advanced topic and appear less often in interviews.
where: Fenwick trees were invented for frequency tables in data compression
Live leaderboards answering “what rank is this score?”
Time-series databases summing ranges of readings
ATLAS.spot: Many range queries mixed with updates, “count of smaller numbers after”.
pr: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

ATLAS.line: Try a choice, go deeper, undo it at a dead end.
ATLAS.idea: Build a solution one decision at a time. If a partial solution can’t possibly work, undo the last decision and try the next option. It’s depth-first search over a tree of choices.
ATLAS.why: It explores every combination systematically, and pruning skips huge parts of the search.
where: Sudoku and puzzle solvers
Constraint solvers for timetables and scheduling
Regular expression engines in languages like Python
SAT solvers, which check chip designs and software for bugs
ATLAS.spot: “All possible”, “every combination or permutation”, “place items so that no two…”.

ATLAS.line: Split the problem, solve the halves, combine.
ATLAS.idea: Break a problem into independent smaller copies, solve them recursively, then merge the answers. When the merge is cheap, the whole thing is fast.
ATLAS.why: It gives many of the fastest known algorithms, and maps naturally onto parallel hardware.
where: Merge sort and quicksort
The fast Fourier transform behind audio, images and wireless

ATLAS.spot: “Construct from halves”, very large inputs that split cleanly, exponentiation.

ATLAS.line: Explore networks ring by ring, or path by path.
ATLAS.idea: A graph is things connected by relationships. Breadth-first search explores outward by distance, so it finds shortest paths when every step costs the same. Depth-first search follows one path as deep as possible before backing up.
ATLAS.why: Maps, networks, grids, dependencies and social connections are all graphs, so this is one of the most reusable skills there is.
where: Web crawlers following links
“People you may know”: friends of friends
Garbage collectors finding every object a program can still reach

ATLAS.spot: A grid of cells, “connected”, “islands”, “minimum number of steps”, “can you reach”.

ATLAS.line: Order tasks so everything comes after what it depends on.
ATLAS.idea: Given “A must happen before B” rules, produce an order that respects them all. It’s only possible when the rules contain no cycle, so the same algorithm also detects circular dependencies.
ATLAS.why: Dependency ordering is everywhere in software and project planning.
where: Build tools like make and Bazel deciding what to compile first

ATLAS.spot: “Prerequisites”, “dependencies”, “order of tasks”, “is it possible to finish”.

ATLAS.line: Track which things belong to the same group, merging as you go.
ATLAS.idea: Each item points toward a representative of its group. Merging two groups and checking whether two items are in the same group are both nearly O(1) with two simple tricks.
ATLAS.why: It answers “are these connected?” over and over as connections are added, faster than re-running a search each time.
where: Kruskal’s algorithm for laying out the cheapest network of cables or roads
Labeling connected regions in images
Type inference in some compilers
Grouping duplicate accounts or records
ATLAS.spot: “Connected components”, “merge accounts”, “redundant connection”, edges arriving one by one.

ATLAS.line: Cheapest routes and cheapest connections.
ATLAS.idea: Dijkstra’s algorithm grows outward from a start, always settling the closest unsettled place next. Bellman-Ford handles negative costs. Minimum spanning trees connect everything for the lowest total cost.
ATLAS.why: Routing and network design are core infrastructure problems.
where: Navigation apps finding driving routes
Internet routing protocols like OSPF, which runs Dijkstra’s algorithm
Pathfinding for game characters and robots, using A*
Planning power grids and cable networks
ATLAS.spot: Weighted edges, “cheapest”, “minimum time for a signal to reach”, “connect all points”.

ATLAS.line: Solve each smaller problem once, and reuse the answer.
ATLAS.idea: When a problem breaks into overlapping subproblems, solve each one once and store it, either top-down with memoization or bottom-up with a table. The hard part is defining the subproblem.
ATLAS.why: Problems that would take exponential time by brute force become polynomial.
where: Spell check and autocorrect, using edit distance

DNA sequence alignment in biology
Decoding noisy signals in phones and speech recognition with the Viterbi algorithm
Laying out paragraphs in typesetting systems like TeX
ATLAS.spot: “Number of ways”, “minimum cost”, “longest or maximum”, choices at each step that affect later ones.

ATLAS.line: Take the best-looking choice now, and never look back.
ATLAS.idea: At each step, make the choice that looks best right now. It only works when you can show local choices add up to the best overall answer, and proving that is the real skill.
ATLAS.why: When it works, it’s the simplest and fastest possible solution.
where: Huffman coding inside ZIP and PNG compression
Dijkstra’s, Prim’s and Kruskal’s algorithms
Scheduling jobs by earliest deadline
Making change with standard coins
ATLAS.spot: “Maximum number of non-overlapping”, “minimum jumps”, “can you reach the end”, problems where sorting first reveals an obvious choice.

ATLAS.line: Find patterns in text without rechecking every position.
ATLAS.idea: Naive search compares the pattern at every position. Smarter methods reuse work, for example a rolling hash that updates in O(1) as a window slides along the text.
ATLAS.why: Text search is one of the most common operations in computing.
where: grep and editors’ find features

Plagiarism and duplicate-content detection
Searching DNA sequences
ATLAS.spot: “Find the first occurrence”, “repeated substrings”, “palindromic substring”.
pr: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String

ATLAS.line: A fixed set of states, and rules for moving between them.
ATLAS.idea: Model a system as a set of states, like filling, washing and spinning, with rules for which input moves it to which state. Parsing problems work the same way: read one character at a time and track what state you’re in.
ATLAS.why: It makes complicated behavior predictable and testable, and it’s how most embedded and protocol code is structured.
where: Appliance controllers in washing machines and microwaves
Network protocols like TCP, which moves through states such as LISTEN and ESTABLISHED
Regular expression engines, and the scanners at the front of compilers
Traffic lights, elevators and vending machines
App screens and game character behavior
ATLAS.spot: “Is this a valid number or format?”, parsing a string character by character, or anything that behaves differently depending on what happened before.

ATLAS.line: Matrix tricks, number theory and careful arithmetic.
ATLAS.idea: These problems test reasoning about coordinates, matrices, primes, remainders and very large numbers, often with a neat insight rather than a data structure.
ATLAS.why: They train precision and show where math meets code.
where: Rotating and transforming images and 3D scenes with matrices
Modular arithmetic and fast exponentiation in RSA and other cryptography
Arbitrary-size number arithmetic in calculators and cryptography
Random number generators
ATLAS.spot: A matrix to rotate or walk in a spiral, primes, “without converting to an integer”, digits.

ATLAS.line: Combine structures to make several operations fast at once.
ATLAS.idea: You’re asked to build a class whose operations all hit a target speed. The answer is usually two structures working together, like a hash map with a linked list, or a hash map with an array.
ATLAS.why: This is closest to real engineering: choosing and combining tools to meet requirements.
where: LRU caches in browsers, CDNs and databases
Rate limiters in APIs
Versioned key-value stores that return a value as of a given time
Social media timelines
ATLAS.spot: “Design a…”, “implement the class”, operations that must each run in O(1).
